extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and practitioners in humour studies, psychology, and psychotherapy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidelines and critical criteria for analysing claims about 'positive humour' and the uses of humour in psychotherapy and Positive Psychology; emphasises methodological, theoretical, rhetorical, and ethical concerns. Useful for researchers, clinicians and critics assessing the evidence and rhetoric around humour's benefits and harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between positive and negative humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'positive (loving, healing) humour' from 'negative (aggressive destructive) humour' (Hageseth) and between humour that 'encourages group solidarity' and 'negative or aggressive humour that separates, divides and excludes' (Lefcourt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assert this dichotomy without justification; treat it as a theoretical claim requiring argument. Beware of assuming the distinction is self-evident; specify criteria used for classifying humour as positive or negative and demonstrate how effects differ rather than merely labelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuinely funny versus hostile humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed distinction that 'genuinely funny' jokes do not depend on 'disparagement' and that 'hostile humour' (ridicule/mockery) should not properly be called humour (Lefcourt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this is a moral as well as empirical claim. Authors should provide theoretical foundations and empirical evidence if asserting that disparagement-based humour is not 'genuine' humour; otherwise acknowledge that many people may find hostile humour funny and explore that tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate humour by its outcomes (health, wellbeing, social effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that humour produces positive outcomes (reduces stress, enhances communication, favors mental and physical health, helps individuals maintain positive affect during negative events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require high-quality empirical evidence before accepting broad claims. Note that reviews cited found the empirical evidence 'generally weak and inconclusive'; beware of small, methodologically flawed studies (e.g., immune-function abstracts) being cited as established fact. Distinguish anecdotal clinical success stories from controlled studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of humour in psychotherapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour 'when used wisely ... can enrich patients' lives and facilitate the psychotherapeutic process' but may be inappropriate for patients with fragile egos or when used callously or at another's expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical guidance should identify contraindications, give concrete examples of inappropriate uses, and present cases where humour produced negative outcomes (not only successful anecdotes). Avoid rhetorical sanitization of potentially harmful therapist remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of power, vulnerability and target harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some humour (ethnic jokes, 'Newfie' jokes, disparagement) can reinforce demeaning stereotypes and contribute to the vulnerability of target groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link illustrative examples (e.g., specific ethnic jokes) explicitly to discussions of harm rather than omitting or downplaying the nature of the joke. Analyse how humour reinforces social hierarchies and the real-world effects on vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and breadth of research topics (include hostile/negative humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research agendas should not favor only the positive benefits of humour; 'aggressive or hostile humour has not been investigated extensively' despite hostility and aggression being major psychological topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure empirical research programs address negative/hostile forms of humour as well as positives, and explain any imbalances rather than assuming them to be neutral or fortuitous. Consider institutional incentives that bias topic selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide negative examples and data (not only positive anecdotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors frequently provide clinical anecdotes of humour leading to improvements but omit stories where humour led to harm or abandonment; the text notes a lack of 'unhappy endings' in clinical write-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advocating humour use, include case studies, transcripts, or data showing inappropriate or harmful outcomes. Explicitly report and analyse failures and near-miss incidents rather than converting them into success narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical masking and euphemisms (the 'Tease-Spray' effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors use softer terms ('teasing', 'liberation', 'just joking') or rhetorical devices to downplay hostility or disparagement in humour—termed here the 'Tease-Spray'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine descriptive language; do not allow euphemisms to neutralize or hide cruelty. Explicitly name hostile acts and analyse their affective and social consequences instead of relabelling them with gentler terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical justification for classifying emotions as positive/negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive Psychology and related accounts list emotions as 'positive' (joy, contentment, amusement) or 'negative' (fear, anger) but often do not specify criteria for these classifications, risking circular reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide non-circular criteria for labeling emotions positive/negative (e.g., measurable consequences, functional roles, cross-contextual effects). Avoid defining 'positive emotions' by the fact that they produce positive outcomes without independent grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to ideological bias (positivism) in framing humour research
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideology of 'accentuating the positives and eliminating the negatives' (positivism) can shape both popular and academic writing, privileging positive findings and downplaying scepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question cultural and institutional motives for privileging positive accounts; explicitly discuss ideological influences on topic choice, interpretation and dissemination (including media distortion of weak findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor for health-related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims linking laughter/humour to immune function or general health have sometimes relied on small, flawed studies or abstracts rather than full, rigorous reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand full reports, replication, adequate sample sizes, appropriate controls and peer review before accepting health-related claims. Note and correct misrepresentation when abstracts are promoted as definitive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit cautionary guidance in applied contexts (caregiving/medical settings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied works sometimes include a short 'A Few Cautions' section advising that health professionals should avoid sarcastic, mocking and degrading humour, but these sections may be brief and lack empirical grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand cautionary guidance into evidence-based protocols: supply specific do/don't examples, sensitivity training, context rules, and data illustrating negative impacts. Avoid tokenistic brief cautions without supporting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize optimistic/positive reappraisal and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive Psychology encourages 'positive reappraisal' and learned optimism, but the text warns this can be problematic (e.g., positive emotions might empower harmful politics) and that 'positive' experiences can have ambivalent or harmful effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse contexts where positive framing may produce maladaptive or harmful outcomes; distinguish types/qualities of 'positive' states and avoid blanket prescriptions that promote optimism as always beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect on researcher/author positionality and career incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers may avoid investigating negative effects of humour because doing so risks professional marginalization (loss of invitations, accusations of bias); this shapes the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit how career incentives and professional communities influence research choices. Encourage institutional support for work that examines harms and challenge practices that discourage such investigations.
